new_statements.quote: ანდიურში გვაქვს სუსტი დინამიკური მახვილი ... მახვილის ადგილი სიტყვაში არ არის ფიქსირებული ერთ რომელიმე მარცვალზე და სიტყვათა ფორმებში შეიძლება იყოს მოძრავი. შეიმჩნევა ტენდენცია მახვილის ადგილის ფიქსირებისა დახურულ მარცვალზე, როცა ასეთი მარცვალი სიტყვაში გვაქვს ...: იხვო́ბ „წისქვილი“, ... ჰა́რკუ „თვალი“ ... თუ სიტყვაში დახურული მარცვალი ერთზე მეტია, მახვილი ჩვეულებრივ მომდევნო (ბოლო) დახურულ მარცვალზეა: გუნგუ́ლ „ქვაბი“, ლენსი́ბ „წარბი“ ... [p. 27] ოდენ ღია მარცვლების შემცველ სიტყვებსა და მათ ფორმებში მახვილის ადგილი თავისუფალია; ჰეკა́ „კაცი“, ვოშო́ „ვაჟიშვილი“ ... მაგრამ: ... მა́ტუ „სარკე“, ო́ხი „ბაღი“
new_statements.translation: In Andi we have a weak dynamic stress ... The place of stress in the word is not fixed on any one syllable and may be mobile across word forms. A tendency is observed for the stress to be fixed on a closed syllable when the word has one ...: ixwób 'mill', ... hárk'u 'eye' ... If the word has more than one closed syllable, stress is usually on the following (last) closed syllable: gungúl 'cauldron', lensíb 'eyebrow' ... [p. 27] In words (and forms) containing only open syllables the place of stress is free: hek'á 'man', wošó 'son' ... but: ... mát'u 'mirror', óxi 'garden'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak dynamic word stress, not fixed to a position: closed syllables attract it, and when several syllables are closed the last closed one carries it (so consonant-final words and forms ending in a consonant-final suffix are end-stressed: k'ótu 'horse' ~ k'otíl 'horses', gédu 'cat' ~ gedobíl 'cats'); in words made only of open syllables the position is lexically free (final hek'á, wošó vs initial mát'u, óxi), with occasional vacillation.
new_statements.exceptions: All-open-syllable words have lexically free stress with some vacillation (bóc'o 'wolf' but oblique boc'ú-); Munib sub-dialect: stress realised mainly by pitch rather than intensity; Dirr 1906 (quoted in fn.) said stress is mostly on the 'first' syllable; Sulejmanov (Rikvani, quoted in fn.) found no determinable fixed stress; Tsertsvadze adds stress causes no vowel reduction. Competing accounts: Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990: 322 deny word stress (phrasal accent on 1st syllable or closed 2nd, plus four syllabic tones); Moroz et al. 2026 (Zilo, preliminary) report initial stress in all-open words and stress on the FIRST closed syllable for most speakers, with pre-stressing and stress-attracting clitics.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly the speech of aul Andi (Andi proper, Upper Andi); author states word stress is weak and often overridden by phrase intonation; examples are citation forms and inflected word forms (plural, aorist, imperative).
new_statements.identity_note: Tsertsvadze's sec. 17 explicitly describes the speech of aul Andi (Andi proper, Upper/'собственно андийский' group); he adds that other sub-dialects also have weak dynamic stress but may differ word-by-word, and that Munib (Lower Andi) has pitch-dominant stress. Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990 also describe village Andi. Moroz et al. 2026 describe Zilo (Upper Andi group) and Salimov 2010 Gagatl. All fall under andi1255; dialect-level glottocodes not verified here.

sources.note: Aul Andi speech: weak dynamic stress (weaker than Avar), barely perceptible, often swamped by phrase stress; place not fixed and mobile across forms; tendency to fall on a closed syllable (ixwób 'mill', hárk'u 'eye'), on the last closed syllable if there are several (gungúl 'cauldron', lensíb 'eyebrow'), hence final in consonant-final words and in forms ending in a C-final suffix (k'ótu 'horse' ~ k'otíl 'horses', gédu ~ gedobíl); in words of open syllables only the place is free/lexical (hek'á 'man', wošó 'son' vs mát'u 'mirror', óxi 'garden'), with occasional vacillation; other sub-dialects…

sources.note: Zilo dialect, preliminary fieldwork results: words of open syllables only -> stress on the first syllable ([ˈxʷari], [ˈk'otu]); most speakers stress the first closed syllable ([ˈhalč'on], [riˈžun]); for some speakers geminates close the syllable; inter-speaker variation whether syllable-closing suffixes (-ij PERF, -ir PROG) attract stress; some clitics/suffixes throw stress onto the preceding syllable (=sːu NEG, =ɬij EQU), others attract it (=esqo PROH, =esːa FUTNEG); Russian loans keep donor stress.

sources.note: Second-hand survey: Andi = unbounded quantity-sensitive stress targeting the rightmost closed syllable (iχwób, hárk'u, gungúl; gédu ~ gedobíl), free in all-open words (hek'á vs mát'u), citing Tsertsvadze 1965: 26-27; notes stress is weak and that Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990: 322 treat the pitch target as phrasal; cites Alekseev 1999a: 221 and Salimov 2010: 19 as identifying word stress; Munib pitch-based stress via Tsertsvadze 1967: 279; K&K four tones for Andi.
